units.markdown:
# Unit 1: Drug discovery, lead discovery and analog based drug design

Making a new medicine is a long, costly and uncertain project. Out of many thousands of compounds that chemists make or buy, only a handful ever reach a patient. Computer aided drug design (CADD) exists to cut down this waste: it helps a team choose which molecules are worth making and testing. Before you can use the computational tools in later units, you need the map of the whole journey — where a **lead** comes from, how it is improved, and what "analog based drug design" means.

## 1.1 Stages of drug discovery and development

```text
Target identification  ->  Target validation  ->  Hit/lead discovery
        -> Lead optimisation -> Preclinical studies -> IND application
        -> Clinical trials Phase I -> II -> III -> Marketing approval
        -> Phase IV (post-marketing surveillance)
```

| Stage | What is done | Typical output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Target identification | Find the enzyme, receptor, ion channel, transporter or nucleic acid whose change causes or controls the disease | A named biological target |
| Target validation | Prove that acting on the target really changes the disease (knockout animals, antisense, tool compounds, clinical genetics) | A "druggable", validated target |
| Assay development | Build a reliable in-vitro test (enzyme inhibition, binding, cell assay) | Screening assay |
| Hit identification | Screen libraries (HTS), natural products, virtual screening, fragment screening | Hits: compounds with measurable activity |
| Lead identification | Confirm hits, check they are real and reproducible, build simple SAR | One or a few lead series |
| Lead optimisation | Improve potency, selectivity, solubility, metabolic stability and safety by making analogs | Preclinical candidate |
| Preclinical | Pharmacology, pharmacokinetics, toxicology in animals, formulation, stability | Data package for the regulator |
| Clinical trials | Phase I safety in healthy volunteers, Phase II efficacy in patients, Phase III large comparative trials | Evidence for approval |
| Regulatory review | Dossier submitted to CDSCO (India), USFDA, EMA | Marketing authorisation |
| Phase IV | Post-marketing surveillance, pharmacovigilance | Long-term safety information |

Useful definitions to quote in the exam:

- **Target** — the macromolecule in the body with which a drug interacts to produce its effect.
- **Hit** — a compound that shows the wanted activity in a screening assay, usually weak.
- **Lead** — a compound with confirmed, reproducible activity, a known structure, acceptable early properties, and clear scope for chemical modification. It is not yet a drug.
- **Drug candidate** — the optimised molecule chosen to go into preclinical and clinical development.
- **Pharmacophore** — the arrangement in space of the structural features needed for activity.

Why the early stages matter so much: a molecule rejected at the design stage costs almost nothing, while one rejected in Phase III costs a fortune. CADD shifts the decision-making to the cheap end of the pipeline, and also reduces the number of animals used.

## 1.2 Rational approaches to lead discovery

**(a) Leads from traditional medicine (ethnopharmacology).** Plants used for centuries in Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and folk practice are screened for the active principle, which then becomes a lead. Classic examples: reserpine from *Rauwolfia serpentina* (used for hypertension), artemisinin from *Artemisia annua* for malaria, quinine from cinchona bark, morphine from opium, digitalis glycosides from foxglove, and vinca alkaloids from *Catharanthus roseus*. Advantage: human use already suggests both activity and some safety. Limitation: isolating and identifying the true active constituent is slow, and yields are often poor.

**(b) Random screening (blind screening).** Every available compound — synthetic, microbial broth, plant extract — is tested in an assay without any prior reason to expect activity. This was the route to many antibiotics, for example streptomycin from soil actinomycetes. Modern high throughput screening (HTS) is random screening done by robots on hundreds of thousands of wells per day, with miniaturised plates and automated readout. Advantage: no assumptions, so genuinely new chemotypes appear. Limitation: very expensive, large hit lists full of false positives (aggregators, assay interferers).

**(c) Non-random (targeted or directed) screening.** Only compounds that have some structural or mechanistic reason to work are screened — analogs of a known active, compounds from a focused library built around a pharmacophore, or molecules from a related therapeutic class. The hit rate is far higher than with random screening, but the chemical novelty is lower.

**(d) Serendipitous discovery.** An unexpected observation is followed up intelligently. Examples: penicillin, when mould contamination cleared a bacterial plate; the hypoglycaemic effect noticed during sulphonamide use, which led to the sulphonylureas; the mood-lifting effect seen with an antitubercular agent, which pointed to the MAO inhibitors; minoxidil's hair growth and sildenafil's effect observed during cardiovascular trials. Serendipity "favours the prepared mind" — the observation has to be recognised as important.

**(e) Lead discovery based on drug metabolism.** A metabolite may be more active, longer acting or safer than the parent. Then the metabolite itself is developed. Examples of this logic: the conversion of an inactive precursor to an active species (prodrug thinking in reverse), oxazepam and desmethyldiazepam as active metabolites of benzodiazepines, fexofenadine as the active metabolite of terfenadine with a better cardiac safety profile, and acetaminophen (paracetamol) as a metabolite of acetanilide and phenacetin. Metabolism studies also warn of **toxic** metabolites, letting the chemist block the vulnerable position.

**(f) Lead discovery based on clinical observation.** A drug given for one indication shows a useful side effect, which becomes the new indication. Examples: aspirin's antiplatelet action, the use of an antiepileptic for neuropathic pain, the discovery of diuretic and antidiabetic actions from sulphonamide therapy, and the anti-angina nitrates. This is also the basis of **drug repurposing**, where an approved drug is re-tested for a new disease — attractive because its safety and pharmacokinetics are already known.

## 1.3 Analog based drug design

Once a lead exists, the chemist makes **analogs** — close structural relatives — to learn which parts of the molecule matter and to improve the profile. The study of how changes in structure change activity is the **structure–activity relationship (SAR)**.

Common analog strategies:

| Strategy | What is changed | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Homologation | Lengthening or shortening a chain by –CH2– units | Tune lipophilicity and fit |
| Chain branching | Straight to branched chain | Change potency and metabolism |
| Ring variation | Open a chain into a ring, expand, contract or fuse rings | Lock conformation, improve selectivity |
| Introduction of substituents | –Cl, –F, –CH3, –OCH3, –NO2, –NH2 | Change electronic and steric properties |
| Stereochemistry | Separate enantiomers, use a rigid analog | Improve potency, cut off-target effects |
| Isosteric/bioisosteric replacement | Swap one group for another of similar properties | Keep activity, improve ADME or patent position |
| Prodrug formation | Add a cleavable group | Improve absorption, taste, stability or site delivery |

## 1.4 Bioisosterism

**Isosteres** (Langmuir) are atoms, ions or molecules with the same number of atoms and the same number and arrangement of valence electrons, so they have similar physical properties — for example N2 and CO, or N3− and NCO−.

**Bioisosteres** are groups or molecules that have similar physical or chemical properties and produce **broadly similar biological effects**. Bioisosteric replacement means exchanging one such group for another in a lead to improve potency, selectivity, duration, solubility or safety, or to get around a patent.

### Classification

**1. Classical bioisosteres** (Grimm's hydride displacement law and Erlenmeyer's extension):

| Class | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Monovalent | –H and –F; –OH and –NH2; –Cl, –Br, –SH, –CF3 (pseudo-halide) |
| Divalent | –O–, –S–, –NH–, –CH2– |
| Trivalent | –CH= and –N= ; –P= and –As= |
| Tetravalent | =C=, =Si=, =N+=, =P+= |
| Ring equivalents | Benzene, thiophene, pyridine, furan, pyrrole |

**2. Non-classical bioisosteres** — the groups do not obey the electron-count rules but still mimic each other's shape, charge distribution or hydrogen bonding:

- Cyclic and non-cyclic replacements: an open chain replaced by a ring that holds the same geometry.
- Acid replacements for –COOH: tetrazole, sulphonamide, hydroxamic acid, acylsulphonamide, phosphonic acid.
- Carbonyl replacements: –C(=O)– by –SO2– or by a sulphoxide.
- Amide replacements: ester, retro-amide, 1,2,4-oxadiazole, olefin.
- Hydrogen replaced by fluorine (similar size, very different electronegativity, blocks metabolism).

### Why bioisosteric replacement is done

1. Increase potency by better fit or better electronics.
2. Improve selectivity between related receptor subtypes.
3. Block a metabolic soft spot (for example put F where hydroxylation occurs).
4. Improve aqueous solubility or membrane permeability.
5. Remove a toxic or unstable group.
6. Produce a patentable new structure.

### Three case studies

**Case study 1 — Fluorine for hydrogen in 5-fluorouracil.** Uracil is the natural pyrimidine. Replacing the hydrogen at position 5 with fluorine gives a molecule the enzyme thymidylate synthase accepts, but the strong C–F bond cannot be broken in the normal way, so the enzyme is blocked. A monovalent classical bioisostere converts a nutrient into an anticancer agent.

**Case study 2 — Ring bioisosterism in the H2 antagonists.** The imidazole ring of histamine was replaced in a stepwise programme: first an imidazole-containing antagonist, then replacement of the ring by furan, and later by a thiazole ring, giving ranitidine and famotidine respectively, together with replacement of the thiourea group by nitroethenediamine and guanidine-type groups. Potency rose and the unwanted effects of the earlier agents fell.

**Case study 3 — Carboxylic acid replaced by tetrazole in the sartans.** The angiotensin II receptor blockers began with carboxylic acid leads that were poorly absorbed. Replacing –COOH with a tetrazole ring (similar pKa and charge, but more lipophilic and metabolically stable) gave orally active drugs such as losartan. This is the standard textbook example of a non-classical acid bioisostere.

(Other acceptable case studies: sulphonamide to sulphonylurea; procaine to lidocaine, where the ester is replaced by the more stable amide; thiophene for benzene in several NSAIDs.)

## 1.5 Where computers enter

- Target validation — bioinformatics, sequence and structure databases (Unit 4).
- Hit finding — virtual screening and docking instead of, or alongside, HTS (Unit 3).
- Lead optimisation — QSAR models guide which analog to make next (Unit 2).
- Property prediction — drug-likeness and ADMET filters remove likely failures early.
- Conformational analysis and energy minimisation give the three-dimensional shapes everything else depends on (Unit 5).

## Remember

1. Order of stages: target identification → validation → hit → lead → optimisation → preclinical → Phase I–III → approval → Phase IV.
2. Hit = weak activity in a screen; lead = confirmed, modifiable, with early SAR; candidate = optimised molecule entering development.
3. Six routes to a lead: traditional medicine, random screening (HTS), non-random screening, serendipity, drug metabolism, clinical observation.
4. Isostere = same number and arrangement of valence electrons; bioisostere = similar properties **and** similar biological action.
5. Classical bioisosteres are grouped as monovalent, divalent, trivalent, tetravalent and ring equivalents; non-classical ones include tetrazole for –COOH and sulphonamide for carbonyl.
6. Keep three case studies ready: 5-fluorouracil (H → F), the H2 antagonist ring changes, and –COOH → tetrazole in losartan.
7. Repurposing an approved drug is fast because safety and pharmacokinetics are already known.

# Unit 2: Quantitative structure activity relationship (QSAR)

SAR tells you *that* a change in structure changes activity. QSAR puts a number on it: it builds a mathematical equation linking measurable properties of a series of molecules to their biological activity, so that the activity of a molecule nobody has made yet can be predicted. This is the oldest and still the most examined part of computer aided drug design.

## 2.1 SAR versus QSAR

| Point | SAR | QSAR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nature | Qualitative | Quantitative |
| Statement | "Adding a chlorine increases activity" | "log(1/C) = 0.87 π + 1.09 σ + 4.19" |
| Based on | Observation, chemical intuition | Statistics (regression) on measured descriptors |
| Needs | A few analogs | A congeneric series, usually 15–20 or more compounds |
| Output | Which groups matter | Predicted activity of untested analogs, with error estimates |
| Risk | Over-generalising from a few compounds | A model that fits the training set but does not predict (over-fitting) |

**Biological activity in QSAR** is always expressed as the logarithm of the reciprocal of the concentration producing a fixed effect: log(1/C), where C is a molar concentration such as IC50, ED50, MIC or Ki. Three reasons: the response is usually log-linear with concentration; a log scale relates directly to free energy of binding (ΔG° = −2.303RT log K); and the reciprocal makes the more potent compound give the larger number.

## 2.2 History and development

| Period | Contribution |
| --- | --- |
| 1860s | Crum-Brown and Fraser: physiological action is a function of chemical constitution, Φ = f(C) |
| 1890s–1900s | Meyer and Overton: narcotic potency of simple organic compounds parallels their oil/water partition coefficient |
| 1930s | Hammett: electronic substituent constant σ and reaction constant ρ for benzene derivatives |
| 1950s | Taft: steric substituent constant Es from ester hydrolysis rates |
| 1964 | Hansch and Fujita: the linear free energy related model combining lipophilic, electronic and steric terms |
| 1964 | Free and Wilson: the additive group-contribution (de novo) model |
| 1970s–80s | Kier and Hall molecular connectivity indices; Topliss decision tree; Craig plots |
| 1988 onwards | 3D-QSAR: CoMFA (Cramer), later CoMSIA (Klebe) |
| Present | Many descriptors, machine learning models, strict external validation |

## 2.3 Types of physicochemical parameters (descriptors)

A **descriptor** is any number that describes part of a molecule's structure or behaviour. The three classical families are lipophilic, electronic and steric.

| Family | Parameter | Symbol | Measures |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lipophilic | Partition coefficient, its logarithm | P, log P | How the molecule shares itself between octanol and water |
| Lipophilic | Substituent lipophilicity constant | π | Lipophilicity contributed by one group |
| Lipophilic | Distribution coefficient | log D | Partition at a stated pH, counting the ionised form |
| Electronic | Hammett constant | σ (σm, σp) | Electron withdrawal or donation through the ring |
| Electronic | Taft polar constant | σ* | Electronic effect in aliphatic systems |
| Electronic | Ionisation constant, dipole moment, HOMO/LUMO energies, partial charges | pKa, μ, E | Charge distribution and reactivity |
| Steric | Taft steric constant | Es | Bulk of a substituent |
| Steric | Molar refractivity | MR | Volume plus polarisability |
| Steric | Verloop STERIMOL parameters | L, B1–B5 | Length and widths in defined directions |
| Steric | Molecular weight, molar volume, surface area | MW, MV, SA | Overall size |
| Topological | Connectivity index, Wiener index, Balaban index | χ, W, J | Branching and shape from the graph of the molecule |
| Others | Hydrogen bond donor/acceptor count, number of rotatable bonds, polar surface area | HBD, HBA, nRB, PSA | Drug-likeness and transport |

### Partition coefficient

P = concentration of the drug in octanol ÷ concentration in water, measured on the **un-ionised** molecule at equilibrium.

- **Experimental determination:** shake-flask method — shake a known amount of drug with equal volumes of water-saturated n-octanol and octanol-saturated water at a fixed temperature, separate, assay both layers (UV, HPLC), take the ratio. Variants: HPLC retention method (log k′ on a C18 column correlates with log P), counter-current and potentiometric titration methods.
- **Theoretical determination:** add fragment or atom contributions — Rekker's fragmental method (log P = Σ f) and the Hansch–Leo method, Crippen's atom-based method. Software gives ClogP (calculated) against measured log P.
- **π (pi) constant:** π_X = log P(R–X) − log P(R–H). A positive π means the group adds lipophilicity (Cl 0.71, CH3 0.56, t-butyl 1.98, CF3 0.88, Br 0.86), a negative π means it adds polarity (OH −0.67, NH2 −1.23, CONH2 −1.49). π values are additive within the same aromatic system, so log P of a new analog can be estimated from the parent.

### Hammett substituent constant

σ_X = log K_X − log K_H, defined from the ionisation of substituted benzoic acids in water at 25 °C.

- Positive σ = electron withdrawing (NO2 para 0.78, CN 0.66, CF3 0.54, Cl 0.23); negative σ = electron donating (OCH3 para −0.27, CH3 −0.17, OH −0.37, NH2 −0.66).
- σm and σp differ because meta groups act mainly by induction while para groups also act by resonance.
- **Hammett equation:** log(K_X/K_H) = ρσ, or log(k_X/k_H) = ρσ for rate constants. ρ (rho) is the reaction constant: it is 1.00 for benzoic acid ionisation by definition; a large positive ρ means the reaction is helped by electron withdrawal.
- Limitation: it applies to aromatic (and some unsaturated) systems only, not to ortho substituents, where steric effects intrude.

### Taft steric constant

Taft separated the mixed effects in aliphatic ester hydrolysis. Using the fact that acid-catalysed hydrolysis is mostly steric and base-catalysed hydrolysis has both steric and electronic components:

- Es = log(k_X/k_CH3) from **acid**-catalysed hydrolysis — a pure steric term; CH3 is the reference at 0, and bulkier groups give more negative Es (H +1.24, CH3 0.00, C2H5 −0.07, i-Pr −0.47, t-Bu −1.54).
- σ* = (1/2.48)[log(k_X/k_CH3)base − log(k_X/k_CH3)acid] — the polar (electronic) term for aliphatic systems.

**Molar refractivity** MR = [(n² − 1)/(n² + 2)] × (MW/d), where n is the refractive index and d the density. It combines volume and polarisability and is widely used when a substituent fits into a polar pocket.

## 2.4 Hansch analysis (the linear free energy related model)

Hansch assumed that drug action occurs in two steps — random walk to the site (controlled by lipophilicity) and binding at the site (controlled by electronic and steric fit) — and that their free energy contributions add up:

```text
log(1/C) = k1 (log P)  + k2 (sigma) + k3 (Es) + k4        (linear form)

log(1/C) = -k1 (log P)^2 + k2 (log P) + k3 (sigma) + k4   (parabolic form)
```

- Use π in place of log P when all compounds come from the same parent.
- The **parabolic** form is used when activity first rises and then falls with lipophilicity. Too polar and the drug never crosses the membrane; too lipophilic and it is trapped in fat or in the first membrane it meets.
- **Optimum lipophilicity:** differentiate and set to zero → log P₀ = k2 ÷ (2k1) for the equation written as log(1/C) = −k1(log P)² + k2 log P + …
- Bilinear model (Kubinyi): log(1/C) = a log P − b log(βP + 1) + c, which fits a sharper peak than a parabola.

### Judging a Hansch equation

| Statistic | Meaning | What is good |
| --- | --- | --- |
| n | Number of compounds | At least 5 compounds per descriptor |
| r or r² | Correlation coefficient | r > 0.9, r² > 0.8 |
| s | Standard error of the estimate | As small as possible, near the experimental error |
| F | Fisher's test of significance | Large; compare with table value |
| q² (cross-validated r²) | Predictive ability by leave-one-out | q² > 0.5 |

### Worked example (teaching data, not from a real series)

Six para-substituted analogs of one parent were tested. π and σ are the standard literature substituent values; the activities below are invented for practice.

| Substituent | π | σp | log(1/C) observed | log(1/C) calculated | Residual |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H | 0.00 | 0.00 | 4.23 | 4.19 | +0.04 |
| CH3 | 0.56 | −0.17 | 4.45 | 4.49 | −0.04 |
| Cl | 0.71 | 0.23 | 5.08 | 5.06 | +0.02 |
| CF3 | 0.88 | 0.54 | 5.52 | 5.54 | −0.02 |
| t-Bu | 1.98 | −0.20 | 5.71 | 5.70 | +0.01 |
| OH | −0.67 | −0.37 | 3.19 | 3.20 | −0.01 |

Multiple linear regression on this set gives

```text
log(1/C) = 0.873 (pi) + 1.090 (sigma) + 4.188
n = 6    r = 0.999    r^2 = 0.999    s = 0.040    F = 1374
```

**Reading the equation:** both coefficients are positive, so activity rises with lipophilicity and with electron withdrawal; the σ coefficient is larger than the π coefficient, so electronic effects dominate here. There is no squared term, so within this narrow π range (−0.67 to 1.98) no optimum has been reached.

**Prediction:** for a bromo analog (π = 0.86, σp = 0.23) the equation predicts log(1/C) = 0.873(0.86) + 1.090(0.23) + 4.188 = **5.19**, so bromo should be a little more active than chloro. That compound is then made and tested — prediction, synthesis, test, re-fit is the QSAR cycle.

### Worked example of the parabolic form

Suppose a series gives log(1/C) = −0.35(log P)² + 1.60 log P + 3.20.

Optimum log P₀ = 1.60 ÷ (2 × 0.35) = **2.29**, and the maximum activity is −0.35(2.29)² + 1.60(2.29) + 3.20 = **5.03**. At log P = 1.0 the predicted activity is 4.45 and at log P = 4.0 it falls to 4.00. The parabola is symmetrical about log P₀, but real data often rise and fall at different rates on the two sides of the optimum, which is why Kubinyi's bilinear model is sometimes preferred.

## 2.5 Free–Wilson analysis (de novo or additive model)

Free and Wilson assumed that each substituent at each position makes a **constant, additive contribution** to the activity, independent of the rest of the molecule:

```text
BA = mu + sum(a_i * X_i)

BA  = biological activity, usually log(1/C)
mu  = activity of the unsubstituted parent (the reference)
a_i = contribution of substituent i at a particular position
X_i = 1 if that substituent is present at that position, otherwise 0
```

A matrix of 1s and 0s is built (an indicator variable for every substituent at every position) and solved by multiple regression.

### Worked example (teaching data)

Two positions were varied: R1 = H, Cl or OCH3 and R2 = H or CH3. Taking the all-hydrogen parent as the reference, μ = 4.10, and the fitted group contributions are a(Cl) = +0.68, a(OCH3) = +0.32 at R1 and a(CH3) = +0.36 at R2.

| R1 | R2 | Calculated log(1/C) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| H | H | 4.10 |
| Cl | H | 4.78 |
| OCH3 | H | 4.42 |
| H | CH3 | 4.46 |
| Cl | CH3 | 5.14 |
| OCH3 | CH3 | 4.78 |

A compound never made, with Cl at R1 and CH3 at R2, would be predicted as 4.10 + 0.68 + 0.36 = 5.14 — the best of the set, so it is the one to synthesise. (This teaching set is perfectly additive, so the residuals are zero; real data always show scatter.)

### Hansch versus Free–Wilson

| Point | Hansch | Free–Wilson |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Basis | Measured physicochemical parameters | Indicator variables for groups |
| Needs parameter values? | Yes, π, σ, Es must be known | No, only the activity data |
| Extrapolation | Can predict a substituent never used, if its π and σ are known | Cannot predict a substituent absent from the training set |
| Interpretation | Tells you *why* (lipophilic, electronic, steric) | Tells you only *how much* each group adds |
| Number of compounds | Fewer needed | Many needed, each substituent must appear several times |
| Non-linear effects | Handled by the squared or bilinear term | Cannot be handled; assumes strict additivity |

The **mixed (Fujita–Ban) approach** combines both: physicochemical terms for the properties that can be measured, indicator variables for the features that cannot.

### Limitations common to both (2D-QSAR)

1. The series must be **congeneric** — one scaffold, one mechanism and one binding mode.
2. Descriptors must be spread out and not correlated with each other (collinearity gives unstable coefficients).
3. Too many descriptors on too few compounds gives chance correlation; keep the ratio of compounds to descriptors at 5:1 or better.
4. Predictions are valid only inside the range of the training data (the "domain of applicability").
5. No three-dimensional information, so stereochemistry and shape are poorly represented. That is what 3D-QSAR was built to fix.

## 2.6 3D-QSAR: CoMFA and CoMSIA

**CoMFA (Comparative Molecular Field Analysis)** relates activity to the **fields** that surround each molecule rather than to single numbers.

Steps:

```text
1. Collect a series with measured activity; build 3D structures.
2. Find the bioactive conformation of each molecule (docking or the most active analog).
3. ALIGN all molecules on a common core - the single most critical step.
4. Put the aligned set in a 3D grid (typically 2 A spacing).
5. At every grid point calculate the interaction with a probe atom
   (sp3 carbon, +1 charge): steric field (Lennard-Jones) and
   electrostatic field (Coulomb). Cut off very large values.
6. Thousands of field values per molecule -> PLS (partial least squares)
   reduces them to a few components; leave-one-out cross-validation gives q^2.
7. Display the result as coloured contour maps around the molecules.
```

**Reading CoMFA maps:** green contours show where more bulk raises activity, yellow where bulk lowers it; blue shows where positive charge (electron-poor groups) helps and red where negative charge helps. The chemist designs the next analog by filling the green and blue regions and avoiding the yellow ones.

**CoMSIA (Comparative Molecular Similarity Indices Analysis)** is the refinement:

| Point | CoMFA | CoMSIA |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fields used | Steric and electrostatic (hydrophobic and H-bond fields can be added) | Five: steric, electrostatic, hydrophobic, hydrogen bond donor, hydrogen bond acceptor |
| Function | Lennard-Jones and Coulomb potentials | Gaussian-type similarity function |
| Behaviour near the atom | Values rise steeply, so cut-offs are needed | Smooth, no singularity, no cut-offs required |
| Maps | Sometimes fragmented, can lie away from the molecule | Smoother, easier to read, lie closer to the molecule |
| Grid sensitivity | More sensitive to grid spacing and orientation | Less sensitive |

Both are validated by q² (leave-one-out), by an external test set, and by y-randomisation (scramble the activities; a genuine model should then collapse).

**Main limitation of 3D-QSAR:** the result depends completely on the alignment and on the conformation chosen. A different, equally reasonable alignment can give a different model.

## 2.7 Validation of any QSAR model

1. **Internal:** leave-one-out or leave-many-out cross-validation (q² > 0.5), bootstrapping.
2. **External:** keep a test set aside (about 20–25 % of compounds) and check the predicted r² (r²pred > 0.6).
3. **Y-randomisation:** shuffle the activity column and refit many times; the scrambled models must be clearly worse.
4. **Applicability domain:** only predict compounds whose descriptors lie inside the training range.
5. Report n, r², s, F and q² with every equation. An equation without statistics is not a QSAR.

## Remember

1. Activity is always log(1/C); C is molar (IC50, ED50, MIC).
2. π_X = log P(RX) − log P(RH); σ_X = log K_X − log K_H for benzoic acids; Es from acid-catalysed ester hydrolysis (CH3 = 0, bigger group = more negative).
3. Hammett equation log(k_X/k_H) = ρσ; ρ = 1.00 for benzoic acid ionisation.
4. Hansch: log(1/C) = −k1(log P)² + k2 log P + k3σ + k4Es + k5; optimum log P₀ = k2/(2k1).
5. Free–Wilson: BA = μ + Σ aᵢXᵢ, additive group contributions, cannot extrapolate to a new substituent.
6. Statistics to quote: n, r (or r²), s, F, q². Rule of thumb — at least five compounds per descriptor.
7. CoMFA = steric + electrostatic fields, Lennard-Jones and Coulomb, PLS, green/yellow and blue/red contours. CoMSIA = five Gaussian similarity fields, smoother maps, no cut-offs.
8. The weakest point of 3D-QSAR is molecular alignment; the weakest point of 2D-QSAR is the need for a congeneric series.

# Unit 3: Molecular modelling and virtual screening techniques

High throughput screening tests real compounds in real plates. **Virtual screening** tests them inside a computer first, so only the promising ones are bought or synthesised. This unit covers the filters (drug-likeness), the two main search strategies (pharmacophore based and docking based), and the way a molecule can be built from nothing inside the binding site (de novo design).

## 3.1 Virtual screening: the idea

**Virtual screening (VS)** is the computational search of a large compound library for molecules most likely to bind a given target, so that a small, enriched subset goes forward for biological testing.

```text
Library (10^5 - 10^7 compounds)
        |  filters: unwanted groups, drug-likeness, duplicates
        v
Filtered library
        |
        +---- ligand-based VS (similarity, pharmacophore, QSAR)  ... when no protein structure
        |
        +---- structure-based VS (docking)                        ... when the 3D structure is known
        v
Ranked hit list (10^2 - 10^3)
        |  visual inspection, chemical sense, diversity, availability
        v
Purchase / synthesise and test (10 - 100 compounds)
```

| | Ligand-based VS | Structure-based VS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Needs | One or more known active ligands | 3D structure of the target (X-ray, NMR, cryo-EM or a homology model) |
| Methods | 2D similarity, fingerprints, pharmacophore search, shape matching, QSAR | Molecular docking and scoring |
| Speed | Very fast | Slower (seconds to minutes per molecule) |
| Finds new scaffolds? | Yes, through "scaffold hopping" | Yes |
| Main weakness | Biased towards the known actives | Scoring functions are approximate; protein flexibility and water are hard |

Advantages of VS over HTS: much cheaper, uses no compound and no reagent, can screen compounds that have not yet been made, and gives a structural hypothesis for why a hit works. Weaknesses: false positives and false negatives, dependence on the quality of the structure, and the fact that a computed score is not a measured affinity.

## 3.2 Drug-likeness screening

Before any expensive calculation, obviously unsuitable molecules are removed. **Drug-likeness** is the extent to which a molecule's properties resemble those of known oral drugs.

**Lipinski's rule of five** (a molecule is likely to have poor oral absorption or permeation if two or more of these are broken):

| Property | Limit |
| --- | --- |
| Molecular weight | not more than 500 |
| log P (calculated) | not more than 5 |
| Hydrogen bond donors (sum of OH and NH) | not more than 5 |
| Hydrogen bond acceptors (sum of N and O) | not more than 10 |

Exceptions are important to mention: natural products, antibiotics, antifungals, vitamins and substrates of active transporters often break the rules and are still good drugs. The rule is about **passive** oral absorption, not about potency.

**Veber's rules** (oral bioavailability in the rat): rotatable bonds ≤ 10 and polar surface area ≤ 140 Å² (or total hydrogen bonds ≤ 12).

**Other common filters**

| Filter | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Ghose filter | MW 160–480, log P −0.4 to 5.6, molar refractivity 40–130, 20–70 atoms |
| Lead-likeness | Smaller and less lipophilic than drugs (MW ≤ 350, log P ≤ 3), leaving room for optimisation |
| Rule of three (fragments) | MW < 300, log P ≤ 3, HBD ≤ 3, HBA ≤ 3, rotatable bonds ≤ 3 |
| REOS / PAINS filters | Remove reactive, unstable or promiscuous groups (Michael acceptors, quinones, rhodanines, catechols, epoxides, acyl halides) that give false positives |
| Ligand efficiency | LE = ΔG ÷ number of heavy atoms; keeps hits small and efficient |

**ADMET prediction** also belongs here: predicted solubility, Caco-2 or MDCK permeability, blood–brain barrier penetration, plasma protein binding, cytochrome P450 inhibition and substrate status, hERG channel blockade (cardiac risk), Ames mutagenicity and hepatotoxicity alerts. Using these early is called "failing fast and failing cheap"; the principle is that poor pharmacokinetics and toxicity, not lack of potency, cause most late-stage failures.

## 3.3 Pharmacophore mapping and pharmacophore based screening

**Pharmacophore** (IUPAC): the ensemble of steric and electronic features that is necessary to ensure the optimal supramolecular interactions with a specific biological target and to trigger (or block) its biological response. In plain words — the pattern of features, and the distances between them, that a molecule must carry to be active. It is an abstraction, **not** a real molecule and not a functional group list.

**Typical pharmacophoric features**

| Feature | Usual symbol / colour | Examples in a molecule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hydrogen bond donor (HBD) | Violet / D | –OH, –NH, –NH2 |
| Hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) | Green / A | C=O, ring N, ether O |
| Hydrophobic (H) | Cyan / yellow | Alkyl chain, phenyl, halogen |
| Aromatic ring / ring aromatic (RA) | Orange | Benzene, pyridine |
| Positive ionisable (PI) | Red | Protonated amine, guanidine |
| Negative ionisable (NI) | Blue | –COO−, tetrazole, phosphate |
| Exclusion volume | Grey sphere | Space occupied by the protein — ligand atoms are forbidden here |

```text
A simple three-point pharmacophore

        HBA
         |  5.2 A
         |
   PI ---+--------- HYD
      7.8 A      6.4 A

A molecule matches if it can place a hydrogen bond acceptor, a positive
ionisable centre and a hydrophobic group at these mutual distances
(within a tolerance, usually about 1 - 1.5 A) in one low-energy conformation.
```

### Pharmacophore mapping (model generation)

**Ligand based** (no protein structure):

1. Collect a set of active molecules, ideally chemically diverse but acting at the same site, with measured activity.
2. Generate many low-energy conformers of each.
3. Superimpose (align) the molecules and look for features common to all.
4. Build the hypothesis: features plus distances plus tolerances.
5. Score and rank the hypotheses, usually by how well they separate actives from inactives.
6. Validate: test against a set of known actives mixed with decoys; measure enrichment.

**Structure based** (protein structure or a ligand–protein complex available): identify the interactions the bound ligand makes in the crystal structure (hydrogen bonds, salt bridge, hydrophobic contacts) and convert them into features; add exclusion volumes from the protein atoms. A pharmacophore built from the empty site alone is called a site-point or apo pharmacophore.

**Pharmacophore based screening:** the hypothesis becomes a 3D query. Every library compound is tested — can it present these features at these distances in some accessible conformation (conformers worked out on the fly or stored in a multi-conformer database)? Matching molecules are kept and ranked by fit value.

**Uses:** fast screening of millions of compounds; **scaffold hopping** (finding a chemically different core that presents the same features, useful for patents and for improving properties); building focused libraries; and as a filter before docking.

**Limitations:** depends on correct alignment and on the set of conformers used; may miss actives whose features sit slightly outside the tolerance; gives no estimate of affinity by itself.

## 3.4 Molecular docking

**Docking** predicts the preferred position, orientation and conformation (together called the **pose**) of a ligand inside the binding site of a macromolecule, and estimates the strength of the interaction with a **scoring function**.

Two parts of every docking program:

1. **Search algorithm** — explores the possible poses (translations, rotations, and for a flexible ligand, the torsions).
2. **Scoring function** — gives each pose a number meant to reflect binding affinity.

### Preparing for docking

```text
Protein                          Ligand
-------                          ------
Get structure (PDB) or build     Draw / retrieve structure
a homology model                 Generate 3D coordinates
Remove water (keep conserved     Add hydrogens, set the correct
waters if they bridge)           protonation and tautomer
Add hydrogens, assign charges    Assign charges, set stereochemistry
Fix missing residues/loops       Energy minimise
Choose and define the grid box
around the active site
```

### Types of docking

| Type | Protein | Ligand | Comment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Rigid docking** (rigid body) | Rigid | Rigid | The oldest approach; the lock-and-key model. Only six degrees of freedom (3 translations + 3 rotations). Very fast, used for shape matching of large databases, and for protein–protein docking. Misses any pose that needs the ligand to change shape. |
| **Flexible ligand docking** | Rigid | Flexible | The standard method today. The induced-fit problem is only partly addressed, but it is a good compromise between accuracy and speed. |
| **Flexible docking (both flexible)** | Flexible (side chains, sometimes loops) | Flexible | Closest to reality (induced fit), but very demanding. Handled by soft potentials, rotamer libraries for side chains, induced-fit protocols, or by docking into several structures (ensemble docking). |
| **Manual docking** | — | — | The user places the ligand in the site by hand with interactive graphics, guided by chemical knowledge and real-time energy feedback, then minimises. Useful for a single well-understood complex and for teaching; not practical for screening and subject to personal bias. |

**How ligand flexibility is handled**

| Approach | Method |
| --- | --- |
| Systematic | Incremental construction: anchor a rigid fragment, then grow the rest bond by bond; or a systematic torsion search |
| Stochastic / random | Monte Carlo, simulated annealing, genetic algorithms (population of poses, crossover and mutation, fitness = score), tabu search |
| Ensemble | Pre-generate many conformers and dock each one rigidly |
| Simulation | Molecular dynamics and energy minimisation inside the site |

### Scoring functions

| Class | Based on | Examples / notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Force-field based | Sum of van der Waals, electrostatic and sometimes solvation terms from a molecular mechanics force field | Physically clear, but desolvation and entropy are poorly treated |
| Empirical | Weighted sum of terms (hydrogen bonds, ionic contacts, hydrophobic contact area, rotatable bonds frozen) with weights fitted to measured affinities of known complexes | Fast; depends on the training set |
| Knowledge-based | Statistical potentials from the frequency of atom-pair contacts observed in the PDB | Robust and fast; implicitly includes effects hard to model |
| Consensus | Combine several scoring functions and keep compounds ranked well by most of them | Reduces the chance of a single function's systematic error |

**Validation of a docking protocol**

- **Re-docking:** remove the ligand from a crystal complex and dock it back. Success is usually taken as **RMSD ≤ 2 Å** from the crystal pose.
- **Cross-docking:** dock a ligand into a structure solved with a different ligand.
- **Enrichment:** dock known actives mixed with decoys and check how many actives appear in the top few per cent (enrichment factor, ROC curve).

**Docking based screening** is simply docking applied to a whole library: filter → dock in a fast mode → re-dock the best few per cent in a careful mode → consensus scoring → visual inspection by a chemist → buy and test.

**Limitations of docking:** scoring functions correlate only moderately with measured affinity (good at ranking poses, weak at ranking molecules); protein flexibility and ordered water molecules are simplified; entropy and desolvation are approximate; protonation and tautomer choices change the result. Always treat a docking score as a hypothesis to be tested in the laboratory.

## 3.5 De novo drug design

**De novo design** builds a brand-new ligand inside the binding site atom by atom or fragment by fragment, instead of searching an existing library.

Steps:

1. Analyse the site — shape, hydrophobic pockets, hydrogen bonding groups, charges.
2. Place **hot spots** or probe fragments where favourable interactions are predicted.
3. **Build** the molecule by one of two strategies:
   - **Linking:** place several fragments in their best sub-pockets, then join them with a suitable linker (the fragment-linking approach).
   - **Growing:** start from one anchored fragment and add atoms or groups stepwise, scoring at each step.
   - (Atom-based growth is possible but gives molecules that are hard to synthesise.)
4. Score and rank the structures built.
5. Filter for drug-likeness and, crucially, for **synthetic accessibility**.
6. Make the best designs and test them.

**Advantages:** truly novel structures (so new patent space), good shape complementarity with the site, useful when libraries contain nothing suitable.

**Limitations:** many of the molecules built cannot realistically be synthesised; scoring errors are magnified because nothing is based on a known active; results depend heavily on the quality of the structure used.

**Fragment based drug design (FBDD)** is the experimental cousin: screen very small fragments (rule of three) by biophysical methods such as NMR, surface plasmon resonance, thermal shift or X-ray crystallography; they bind weakly but efficiently, and are then grown, linked or merged into a lead. Ligand efficiency is the guiding number.

## 3.6 Putting the methods together

| Situation | Best approach |
| --- | --- |
| Protein structure unknown, several actives known | Ligand-based: pharmacophore, similarity, QSAR |
| Protein structure known, no ligand known | Structure-based: docking, de novo design |
| Both known | Structure-based pharmacophore, docking validated by re-docking, then QSAR on the hits |
| Need a new scaffold for patent reasons | Pharmacophore based scaffold hopping, or de novo design |
| Library of millions, limited computer time | Filter → pharmacophore screen → dock the survivors |

## Remember

1. Virtual screening ranks compounds in the computer so that only an enriched subset is tested; ligand-based needs known actives, structure-based needs the 3D target.
2. Lipinski: MW ≤ 500, log P ≤ 5, HBD ≤ 5, HBA ≤ 10 — about passive oral absorption, with well-known exceptions. Veber adds rotatable bonds ≤ 10 and PSA ≤ 140 Å².
3. A pharmacophore is a pattern of features (HBD, HBA, hydrophobic, aromatic, positive and negative ionisable) with distances and tolerances, plus exclusion volumes — never a real molecule.
4. Docking = search algorithm + scoring function; output is a pose plus a score.
5. Rigid (lock and key) → flexible ligand (standard) → both flexible (induced fit); manual docking is done by hand on graphics.
6. Scoring functions: force-field, empirical, knowledge-based, consensus.
7. Re-docking success is judged by RMSD ≤ 2 Å against the crystal pose; screening success by enrichment factor.
8. De novo design grows or links fragments inside the site; its main practical problem is synthetic accessibility.

# Unit 4: Informatics and methods in drug design

Every method in the earlier units needs data — protein sequences and structures, molecular structures, measured activities, measured ADME properties. Informatics is the organised storage, retrieval and analysis of that data. Two branches matter for drug design: **bioinformatics** (biological molecules — DNA, RNA, proteins) and **chemoinformatics** (small molecules and their properties).

## 4.1 Introduction to bioinformatics

**Bioinformatics** is the use of computer methods to store, retrieve, analyse and interpret biological data, mainly nucleic acid and protein sequences, structures and functions.

**Why a drug designer needs it**

| Task | Bioinformatics tool |
| --- | --- |
| Find and choose a target | Genome and proteome databases, disease–gene links |
| Check how similar the target is to other human proteins | Sequence alignment — predicts selectivity problems and side effects |
| Get the 3D structure | Structure databases; if none exists, build a homology model |
| Find the binding site | Structural comparison with related proteins, cavity detection |
| Understand pathways | Pathway and interaction databases |
| Personalised medicine | Polymorphism data (for example variation in drug-metabolising enzymes) |

**Core ideas**

- **Sequence alignment** — writing two or more sequences one under the other to show matching residues. *Pairwise* alignment compares two sequences; *multiple* alignment compares several and shows conserved regions. **BLAST** is the standard fast search tool: it compares a query sequence with a whole database and reports similar sequences with scores and E-values (a low E-value means the match is unlikely to be chance). **Clustal** type programs do multiple alignment.
- **Homology (comparative) modelling** — building the 3D structure of a protein from the known structure of a related protein. Steps: find a template with high sequence identity (ideally above 30 %), align target and template, copy the conserved backbone, build loops and side chains, energy minimise, then validate (Ramachandran plot, stereochemistry checks). Used when no experimental structure exists — very common for G-protein coupled receptors and for many bacterial and parasite enzymes.
- **Structural genomics and proteomics** — large-scale determination of structures and of the protein complement of a cell.
- **Phylogenetic analysis** — evolutionary trees; useful to see whether a parasite enzyme has a close human relative (if not, a selective drug is more likely).

### Important biological databases

| Database | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| GenBank (NCBI), EMBL-ENA, DDBJ | Nucleotide sequences; the three exchange data daily |
| UniProt (Swiss-Prot reviewed + TrEMBL unreviewed) | Protein sequences with curated annotation |
| Protein Data Bank (PDB, run by the wwPDB with RCSB, PDBe and PDBj) | Experimentally determined 3D structures of proteins and nucleic acids (X-ray, NMR, cryo-EM) |
| Cambridge Structural Database (CSD) | Small-molecule crystal structures — bond lengths, angles, preferred conformations |
| Pfam, InterPro | Protein families and domains |
| SCOP, CATH | Structural classification of proteins |
| KEGG, Reactome | Metabolic and signalling pathways |
| BRENDA | Enzyme data — substrates, inhibitors, kinetics |
| PubMed / MEDLINE | Biomedical literature |
| Ensembl, UCSC Genome Browser | Genome annotation |

A PDB entry is identified by a four-character code and contains the atomic coordinates, the resolution, the R-factor, the bound ligands (HETATM records) and the crystallographic water. Resolution matters: below about 2.0 Å the structure is detailed enough for careful docking; above 3.0 Å side-chain positions are uncertain.

## 4.2 Introduction to chemoinformatics

**Chemoinformatics (cheminformatics)** is the application of computer methods to chemical problems: representing, storing, searching and analysing chemical structures and their biological and physical data.

### Representing a molecule in a computer

| Representation | What it is | Example / note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Connection table | List of atoms and the bonds between them | The basis of MOL and SDF files |
| **SMILES** | A single line of text for a structure | Ethanol CCO; benzene c1ccccc1; aspirin CC(=O)Oc1ccccc1C(=O)O |
| **SMARTS** | A pattern language for substructure searching | Used to write filters for unwanted groups |
| **InChI / InChIKey** | A standard, non-proprietary identifier; the InChIKey is a fixed-length hashed version | Good for looking a compound up across databases |
| MOL / SDF | Single and multiple structure files with coordinates and data fields | The usual exchange format for libraries |
| MOL2, PDB | Formats carrying 3D coordinates, atom types and charges | Used by docking programs |
| Fingerprints | A string of bits recording which fragments are present | MACCS keys (fixed set of substructures), path-based and circular (ECFP) fingerprints |

### Searching

- **Exact search** — the same compound (best done through InChIKey or a canonical SMILES).
- **Substructure search** — all compounds containing a given fragment; uses graph matching, speeded up by screening with fingerprints first.
- **Similarity search** — compounds "like" a query. Similarity between two fingerprints is usually the **Tanimoto coefficient**: Tc = c ÷ (a + b − c), where a is the number of bits set in molecule A, b in molecule B and c the number set in both. Tc runs from 0 to 1; above about 0.85 with a good fingerprint, two molecules are usually considered similar. The **similar property principle** says structurally similar molecules usually have similar properties — the basis of ligand-based screening, but it fails at "activity cliffs", where a tiny change destroys activity.
- **Pharmacophore and 3D shape search** — described in Unit 3.

### Other chemoinformatics jobs

- Library design (diverse libraries, focused libraries, combinatorial enumeration).
- Calculation of descriptors and properties (log P, PSA, pKa, solubility).
- Duplicate removal, salt stripping, tautomer and protonation standardisation — the unglamorous but essential cleaning of data.
- Clustering and diversity analysis, so that the compounds bought represent the whole chemical space.
- Data mining of screening results and electronic laboratory notebooks.

## 4.3 ADME databases and predictive tools

ADME (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion) and toxicity data decide whether an active molecule can ever become a medicine. Databases collect measured values; predictive tools estimate them from structure.

**Properties stored or predicted**

| Step | Typical parameters |
| --- | --- |
| Absorption | Aqueous solubility, log P and log D, PSA, Caco-2 or MDCK permeability, human intestinal absorption, P-glycoprotein substrate/inhibitor |
| Distribution | Plasma protein binding, volume of distribution, blood–brain barrier penetration |
| Metabolism | Cytochrome P450 isoform (CYP1A2, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6, 3A4) substrate and inhibitor status, metabolic sites, half-life |
| Excretion | Renal clearance, total clearance |
| Toxicity | hERG inhibition (QT prolongation risk), Ames mutagenicity, hepatotoxicity, skin sensitisation, acute toxicity class |

**Resources commonly named in textbooks**

| Resource | Content |
| --- | --- |
| admetSAR | Collected ADMET data with prediction models |
| SwissADME | Free web calculation of physicochemical properties, drug-likeness, pharmacokinetic behaviour |
| pkCSM | Predicts ADMET endpoints from graph-based signatures |
| DrugBank | Drug entries combining chemistry, pharmacology, targets, metabolism and interactions |
| Metrabase, drug metabolism databases | Transporter and metabolism data |
| PharmGKB | Pharmacogenomic data — how genetic variation changes drug response |
| PubChem (BioAssay section) | Screening results, including toxicity assays |

**How these are used:** apply them as filters right after drug-likeness screening, and again on the final docking hits; a potent compound predicted to block hERG, to be a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor or to be mutagenic is deprioritised before any chemistry is done. Remember that these are *predictions* with limited accuracy, especially for metabolism; they guide experiments, they do not replace them.

## 4.4 Chemical, biochemical and pharmaceutical databases

| Type | Database | Content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chemical | **PubChem** (NCBI) | Very large open collection of compound structures, properties and bioassay results |
| Chemical | **ChemSpider** | Open structure search across many sources |
| Chemical | **CAS Registry / SciFinder** | Every compound indexed with a CAS Registry Number; the commercial standard for literature and reaction searching |
| Chemical | **Reaxys** (formerly Beilstein and Gmelin) | Reactions, preparations and measured properties |
| Chemical | **ZINC** | Commercially available compounds, ready-prepared in 3D for virtual screening |
| Chemical | **Cambridge Structural Database** | Small-molecule crystal structures |
| Biochemical / bioactivity | **ChEMBL** | Measured bioactivities (IC50, Ki, EC50) from the medicinal chemistry literature, linked to targets |
| Biochemical / bioactivity | **BindingDB** | Measured binding affinities of ligand–protein pairs |
| Biochemical | **BRENDA**, **KEGG**, **Reactome** | Enzymes, pathways, reactions |
| Biochemical / structure | **PDB**, **PDBbind** | Structures; PDBbind adds measured affinities for complexes |
| Target | **Therapeutic Target Database**, **SuperTarget** | Known and explored drug targets with their drugs |
| Pharmaceutical | **DrugBank** | Approved and investigational drugs: structure, target, mechanism, pharmacokinetics, interactions |
| Pharmaceutical | **USFDA Orange Book**, **Drugs@FDA**, national regulatory databases | Approved products, patents and exclusivity, labelling |
| Pharmaceutical | Pharmacopoeias in electronic form (IP, BP, USP) | Official standards, monographs, tests |
| Clinical | **ClinicalTrials.gov**, **CTRI (Clinical Trials Registry – India)** | Registered clinical trials and their results |
| Safety | **VigiBase / national pharmacovigilance databases** | Reports of suspected adverse drug reactions |
| Natural products | Natural product collections, including Indian ones such as **IMPPAT** for Indian medicinal plant phytochemicals | Structures and sources of natural compounds |
| Literature | **PubMed**, **Google Scholar** | Published papers and abstracts |

**Choosing a database for a task**

```text
Need a 3D protein structure          -> PDB
Need many purchasable molecules in 3D -> ZINC
Need measured IC50 / Ki values        -> ChEMBL, BindingDB
Need drug + target + metabolism facts -> DrugBank
Need any compound's properties quickly-> PubChem, ChemSpider
Need a synthesis route                -> Reaxys, SciFinder
Need pathway context                  -> KEGG, Reactome
Need ADMET estimates                  -> admetSAR, SwissADME, pkCSM
```

### Quality of data

Databases differ in **curation**. Curated resources (Swiss-Prot, ChEMBL, DrugBank) have been checked by people; automatically assembled resources have more errors — wrong stereochemistry, wrong salt forms, duplicate entries, activities recorded in mixed units. Before any QSAR or machine-learning work, data must be standardised: one entry per compound, one unit for activity, salts and solvates stripped, tautomers normalised, suspicious values checked against the original paper. A QSAR model is only as good as the numbers it is fitted to.

## 4.5 Putting informatics into the design cycle

```text
Disease  -> genomics / proteomics          -> target chosen         (bioinformatics)
Target   -> PDB or homology model          -> binding site defined  (bioinformatics)
Site     -> ZINC / in-house library        -> virtual screening     (chemoinformatics)
Hits     -> ChEMBL, BindingDB              -> known SAR checked     (chemoinformatics)
Leads    -> ADMET tools, DrugBank          -> liabilities predicted (ADME databases)
Candidate-> CTRI / ClinicalTrials.gov      -> trial planned
```

## Remember

1. Bioinformatics handles biological macromolecules; chemoinformatics handles small molecules.
2. BLAST = fast sequence similarity search, judged by score and E-value; Clustal-type programs do multiple alignment.
3. Homology modelling needs a template, ideally above 30 % sequence identity, and is validated with a Ramachandran plot.
4. PDB = 3D structures of macromolecules (four-character code, resolution matters); CSD = small-molecule crystal structures.
5. Structure representations: SMILES (line notation), SMARTS (search patterns), InChI/InChIKey (standard identifier), SDF/MOL2/PDB (files with coordinates), fingerprints (MACCS, ECFP).
6. Tanimoto coefficient Tc = c/(a + b − c); the similar property principle underlies similarity searching, and activity cliffs are its exception.
7. ChEMBL and BindingDB hold measured affinities; ZINC holds purchasable compounds ready for docking; DrugBank links drugs, targets and metabolism; PubChem is the large open general resource.
8. Predicted ADMET (solubility, permeability, CYP, hERG, Ames) is a filter, not a measurement — clean, curated data is the foundation of every model.

# Unit 5: Molecular modelling — mechanics, quantum methods, energy minimisation and conformational analysis

Docking, pharmacophore mapping and 3D-QSAR all assume we know what a molecule actually looks like in three dimensions and how much energy each shape costs. This unit supplies that foundation: the two ways of calculating molecular energy (molecular mechanics and quantum mechanics), how a structure is relaxed to a minimum, and how the biologically relevant shape is found among the many a flexible molecule can adopt.

## 5.1 What molecular modelling means

**Molecular modelling** is the use of theoretical and computational methods to build, display and calculate the structures, properties and behaviour of molecules. It answers questions such as: what is the lowest-energy shape of this drug? Where is its negative charge concentrated? How much energy is needed to rotate this bond? How well does it fit this receptor?

Two levels of theory are used:

| | Molecular mechanics (MM) | Quantum mechanics (QM) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Treats the molecule as | Balls (atoms) joined by springs (bonds) — classical physics | Nuclei and electrons, solving the Schrödinger equation |
| Electrons | Not treated explicitly | Treated explicitly |
| Speed | Very fast; thousands of atoms, long simulations | Slow; tens to a few hundred atoms |
| Can it break or form bonds? | No (bond types are fixed) | Yes |
| Gives | Geometry, strain energy, conformational energy | Geometry plus electron density, orbitals, charges, spectra, reaction paths |
| Typical use in drug design | Energy minimisation, conformational search, docking, molecular dynamics, whole proteins | Partial charges, HOMO/LUMO, electrostatic potential maps, small-molecule geometry, mechanism studies |

## 5.2 Molecular mechanics and the force field

A **force field** is the set of equations and the parameters (equilibrium bond lengths, angles, force constants, atomic charges, van der Waals radii) used to calculate the potential energy of a molecule from its geometry.

```text
E(total) = E(bond stretching)
         + E(angle bending)
         + E(torsion / dihedral)
         + E(out-of-plane / improper)
         + E(van der Waals)
         + E(electrostatic)
         ( + E(hydrogen bond), + cross terms, + solvation term )

bonded terms: the first four      non-bonded terms: the last two
```

| Term | Usual equation | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bond stretching | Eb = Σ kb(l − l0)² | Hooke's law spring; l0 is the natural bond length. (A Morse function is more accurate but slower.) |
| Angle bending | Eθ = Σ kθ(θ − θ0)² | Resistance to opening or closing a bond angle |
| Torsion | Eφ = Σ (Vn/2)[1 + cos(nφ − γ)] | Energy as a bond is rotated; n is the periodicity (3 for ethane), γ the phase |
| Out-of-plane | Harmonic penalty | Keeps sp² centres and aromatic rings flat |
| van der Waals | Lennard-Jones 12-6: E = ε[(r0/r)¹² − 2(r0/r)⁶] | Steep repulsion when atoms clash, weak attraction (London forces) at longer range |
| Electrostatic | Coulomb: E = qiqj/(4πε0 εr r) | Attraction or repulsion between partial charges; a distance-dependent dielectric is often used to imitate water |

**Important properties of MM energies**

- The number is a **steric (strain) energy**, meaningful only when comparing conformers or isomers of the **same** molecule with the **same** force field. It is not a heat of formation and cannot be compared between force fields.
- Parameters are fitted to experimental data (crystal structures, spectra) and to QM calculations. A molecule with unusual atoms may be outside the parameter set — then the program guesses, and the result is unreliable.

**Common force fields:** MM2, MM3 and MM4 (small organic molecules, very accurate geometries), AMBER and CHARMM (proteins and nucleic acids, also used for drug–protein systems), GROMOS (simulations), OPLS (liquids and proteins), MMFF94 (broad coverage of drug-like organics), UFF and DREIDING (generic, cover nearly the whole periodic table but with lower accuracy).

## 5.3 Quantum mechanics methods

QM solves (approximately) the Schrödinger equation HΨ = EΨ under the Born–Oppenheimer approximation (nuclei fixed, electrons move around them).

| Class | Approach | Examples | Comment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Ab initio** | From first principles, no experimental parameters | Hartree–Fock (HF); beyond-HF methods such as MP2 and coupled cluster | Most rigorous and most expensive; needs a **basis set** (STO-3G minimal, 3-21G, 6-31G*, 6-311++G**; polarisation functions * and diffuse functions + improve accuracy) |
| **Semi-empirical** | Simplified QM — valence electrons only, many integrals replaced by parameters fitted to experiment | CNDO, INDO, MINDO/3, MNDO, AM1, PM3 | Hundreds of times faster than ab initio; good for geometries, heats of formation and charges of ordinary organic molecules; poor for unusual bonding |
| **Density functional theory (DFT)** | Energy expressed as a functional of the electron density instead of the wave function | B3LYP, M06, PBE with similar basis sets | Accuracy near good ab initio at much lower cost; the usual choice today for medium-sized molecules |
| **Hybrid QM/MM** | The reactive site treated by QM, the rest of the protein by MM | Used for enzyme mechanisms | Lets a reaction be studied inside a whole protein |

**What QM gives a drug designer**

- Accurate geometries and relative energies, including strained or conjugated systems.
- **Partial atomic charges** (Mulliken, electrostatic-potential-derived) used later in docking and MM calculations.
- **Molecular electrostatic potential (MEP) maps** — coloured surfaces showing where a molecule is electron-rich (red, attracts positive charge or donates to an H-bond acceptor) and electron-poor (blue).
- **Frontier orbitals**: HOMO (highest occupied) relates to electron-donating ability, LUMO (lowest unoccupied) to electron-accepting ability; the HOMO–LUMO gap relates to reactivity and stability. These appear as descriptors in QSAR.
- Dipole moment, polarisability, ionisation potential, electron affinity.
- Transition states and reaction energetics (mechanism of an enzyme, stability of a prodrug).

## 5.4 Energy minimisation (geometry optimisation)

A structure drawn on screen or taken from a database has unrealistic bond lengths and clashes. **Energy minimisation** adjusts the coordinates step by step until the net force on every atom is essentially zero — a point where the first derivative of energy with respect to the coordinates is zero and the second derivative is positive (a minimum, not a maximum or saddle point).

```text
Energy
  |        X start
  |         \
  |          \      local minimum
  |           \____/\
  |                  \        global minimum
  |                   \______/
  +-------------------------------------> geometry (one coordinate)

Minimisation only runs downhill, so it always lands in the nearest
minimum - not necessarily the lowest one.
```

| Method | Derivatives used | How it works | Points to remember |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Steepest descent** | First | Move along the direction of the steepest downhill gradient; repeat | Very robust, excellent for a badly strained starting structure; converges slowly near the minimum because successive steps are at right angles and it zig-zags |
| **Conjugate gradient** | First | Each new direction takes the previous ones into account, avoiding zig-zag | Faster convergence than steepest descent; the usual workhorse, often run after a few hundred steps of steepest descent |
| **Newton–Raphson** | First and second (Hessian) | Uses curvature to jump close to the minimum in few steps | Converges very fast near a minimum, but the Hessian is expensive (memory grows with the square of the number of atoms) and it can fail far from the minimum |
| **Quasi-Newton (BFGS, adopted-basis NR)** | First, with an estimated Hessian | Builds up curvature information as it goes | Good compromise, widely used in practice |

**Convergence criteria:** the run stops when the energy change between steps, or the root-mean-square gradient, falls below a set value, or when a maximum number of steps is reached.

**Practical sequence:** clean the structure → add hydrogens → assign the force field → steepest descent (removes bad contacts) → conjugate gradient (refines) → check the final geometry and gradient.

**The key limitation:** minimisation is a downhill-only procedure. It finds the **local** minimum nearest the starting point. Finding the **global** minimum needs a search method (Section 5.6).

## 5.5 Conformational analysis

**Conformers** are the different arrangements of the same molecule produced by rotation about single bonds, without breaking any bond.

- A molecule with N atoms has 3N − 6 internal degrees of freedom (3N − 5 if linear); for a 20-atom molecule that is 54.
- The practical variables are the **rotatable (torsion) bonds**. If each rotatable bond is sampled at only three staggered positions, 5 rotatable bonds give 3⁵ = 243 conformers and 10 give 3¹⁰ = 59,049. This explosion is why systematic searching fails for flexible molecules.

**Potential energy surface (PES):** a plot of energy against the geometric variables. Minima are stable conformers; the highest point on the lowest path between two minima is the **transition state** (rotational barrier).

```text
Ethane, rotation about C-C          n-Butane, rotation about C2-C3

E |   /\      /\      /\            E |    /\      ___      /\
  |  /  \    /  \    /  \             |   /  \    /   \    /  \
  | /    \__/    \__/    \            |__/    \__/     \__/    \__
  +---------------------------->      +----------------------------->
  0   60  120 180 240 300 360         0   60  120 180 240 300 360

Minima at 60, 180, 300 (staggered)   anti (180) lowest; two gauche
Maxima at 0, 120, 240 (eclipsed)     minima (60, 300) slightly higher
```

Standard results you should be able to state: ethane has a three-fold barrier of about 3 kcal/mol (12 kJ/mol); n-butane's anti conformer is the most stable, the gauche conformers are a little higher, and the syn (fully eclipsed) arrangement is the highest point; cyclohexane prefers the chair, with the twist-boat and boat much higher, and a bulky substituent prefers the equatorial position.

**Boltzmann populations.** At equilibrium the ratio of two conformers is N2/N1 = exp(−ΔE/RT). At 25 °C (298 K, RT ≈ 0.59 kcal/mol):

| ΔE (kcal/mol) | Share of the higher conformer | Share of the lower conformer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0.5 | about 30 % | about 70 % |
| 1.0 | about 16 % | about 84 % |
| 2.0 | about 3 % | about 97 % |
| 3.0 | under 1 % | over 99 % |

So differences of 2–3 kcal/mol already decide which shape a molecule is in — but note that the **bioactive conformation** (the shape bound to the receptor) is often *not* the global minimum. The binding energy released can pay for a strain of a few kcal/mol, so conformers within roughly 5–10 kcal/mol of the minimum are all kept as candidates for docking.

**Ways to study conformation**

- Experimental: X-ray crystallography (the solid-state conformation), NMR coupling constants and NOE (solution conformation), the Cambridge Structural Database for preferred torsion values.
- Computational: torsion driving (rotate one bond in fixed steps and minimise the rest at each step), full conformational search, molecular dynamics.

**Ramachandran plot** — for proteins, a plot of the backbone torsions φ (phi) against ψ (psi) showing the allowed regions (right-handed α-helix, β-sheet, left-handed helix). It is the standard check on the quality of a protein structure or a homology model.

## 5.6 Finding the global conformational minimum

The **multiple-minimum problem**: the number of minima grows roughly exponentially with the number of rotatable bonds, so the lowest one cannot be found simply by minimising once.

| Method | How it searches | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Systematic (grid) search** | Rotate every rotatable bond through fixed increments and minimise each combination | Complete and reproducible for rigid or nearly rigid molecules; impossible beyond about 6–8 rotatable bonds (combinatorial explosion). Tree pruning and rules reduce the cost |
| **Monte Carlo** | Make a random change to a torsion, accept it if the energy falls; if it rises, accept with probability exp(−ΔE/kT) (the Metropolis criterion) | The uphill moves let it escape local minima |
| **Simulated annealing** | Monte Carlo (or dynamics) starting at a high temperature and cooling slowly | Mimics the annealing of a metal; widely used in docking and structure refinement |
| **Molecular dynamics (MD)** | Solve Newton's equations of motion in small time steps (typically 1–2 fs) at a chosen temperature; the molecule explores the surface over time | Gives motion and time-dependent behaviour; high temperature runs help cross barriers; snapshots are then minimised |
| **Genetic algorithm** | A population of conformers encoded as "chromosomes" of torsion angles; selection, crossover and mutation across generations | Efficient for flexible ligands; used by several docking programs |
| **Distance geometry** | Generate coordinates from allowed interatomic distance ranges, then minimise | Used in NMR structure determination and in some conformer generators |
| **Low-mode / normal-mode search** | Follow the soft vibrational modes out of a minimum, then minimise again | Good at finding related minima efficiently |

**Practical routine:** generate many conformers by one of the above → minimise each → remove duplicates (by RMSD) → keep everything within an energy window of the lowest → use this set for pharmacophore searching, 3D-QSAR alignment or ensemble docking.

**Important cautions**

1. No search method can *prove* that the global minimum has been found; confidence comes from repeating the search from different starting points and seeing the same lowest structure appear again and again.
2. Most routine calculations are done in the gas phase. Water changes relative energies a great deal — intramolecular hydrogen bonds that dominate in vacuum often open up in water. Use a solvation model (implicit continuum or explicit water) when the answer matters.
3. Garbage in, garbage out: wrong protonation state, wrong tautomer, wrong stereochemistry or a missing parameter will produce a confident but meaningless number.

## Remember

1. MM = balls and springs, no electrons, fast, cannot break bonds. QM = electrons included, slow, can study reactions and gives charges, HOMO/LUMO and MEP maps.
2. Force field terms: bond stretch + angle bend + torsion + out-of-plane (bonded) and van der Waals + electrostatic (non-bonded). Lennard-Jones 12-6 for van der Waals, Coulomb for electrostatics.
3. Name force fields: MM2/MM3, AMBER, CHARMM, OPLS, GROMOS, MMFF94. MM strain energy is comparable only within the same molecule and the same force field.
4. QM classes: ab initio (HF, basis sets such as STO-3G and 6-31G*), semi-empirical (CNDO, MINDO, MNDO, AM1, PM3), DFT (B3LYP), and QM/MM hybrids.
5. Minimisation methods: steepest descent (first derivative, robust, slow near the end), conjugate gradient (first derivative, no zig-zag), Newton–Raphson (second derivative, fast near the minimum, expensive Hessian). All go downhill only, so they stop at the nearest local minimum.
6. Conformers arise from rotation about single bonds; 3N − 6 degrees of freedom; three positions per rotatable bond give 3ⁿ combinations.
7. N2/N1 = exp(−ΔE/RT); about 2 kcal/mol already gives a 97:3 split at room temperature. The bioactive conformation need not be the global minimum, so keep a window of low-energy conformers.
8. Global search methods: systematic grid, Monte Carlo (Metropolis criterion), simulated annealing, molecular dynamics, genetic algorithms, distance geometry, low-mode search.
